blocks: Home
/About Us
More than 30 years of combined team experience
Damtech provides dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage solutions for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties across South Africa.

Damtech provides dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage solutions for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties across South Africa. We install HDPE and PVC dam linings on farms and mines, build corrugated steel reservoirs, and apply bitumen waterproofing on roofs and foundations, always with an emphasis on workmanship you can inspect, not promises you cannot keep.

We are Damtech — specialists in earth dam linings, waterproofing and steel water storage tanks. The Damtech team brings more than 30 years of combined experience across dam linings, waterproofing and water-storage projects. We deliver practical solutions that safeguard your investment and support long-term performance.

Andre has worked in dam lining, waterproofing and water-storage installations since the late 1990s. His experience includes HDPE, PVC, bitumen, steel tanks and concrete roofs across South Africa. At Damtech, he is responsible for site assessment, project supervision, installation, quality checks and client coordination.

To provide top-tier waterproofing and lining solutions that stand the test of time. We strive to exceed our clients' expectations by offering reliable, effective and tailored services — whether you need advanced earth dam linings for large-scale dams or expert waterproofing for roofs and foundations.
Digital platform built by Koppie Systems.
Practical dam linings, waterproofing and water storage solutions.
WHY DAMTECH
Damtech delivers practical dam linings, waterproofing and water storage solutions with a focus on long-term leak prevention and reliable workmanship.
Proudly based in South Africa, with practical understanding of local site conditions, climate and client requirements.
Decades of experience in dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage for farms, mines and commercial sites.
Dam linings, steel water tanks and waterproofing projects for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties nationwide.
Practical solutions for agricultural, mining, estate and commercial water storage with supplier-backed materials where applicable.

Our teams have lined irrigation dams in the Western Cape, built steel tanks for Mpumalanga citrus farms, and repaired torch-on roofs on Gauteng commercial stores. That range helps us understand regional soils, rainfall patterns and the pressure load-shedding puts on borehole and pumping schedules, which shapes how we specify liners and tank sizes.

We listen first: what water you need to store, how you use it, and what has failed before. Then we recommend materials and thicknesses that fit the site, not whatever is cheapest to freight. Installation crews prepare substrates properly, weld and anchor to spec, and leave you with maintenance guidance. After handover we are still a phone call away for inspections, patches and expansions.
OUR SERVICES
Dam linings, steel water tanks and waterproofing for farms, mines and commercial properties.
HDPE, PVC and bitumen torch-on lining for agricultural farm dams, mining ponds and irrigation storage nationwide.
Corrugated galvanised reservoirs from 11 kL to 500 kL+ with PVC lining, columns and optional roofs.
Bitumen torch-on and maintenance for roofs, foundations and retaining structures on farms and commercial buildings.
WHAT WE DELIVER
Steel water storage tanks with custom sizes, roofs and support columns
HDPE geomembrane linings for large gravel and farm dams
PVC linings for ponds and zinc reservoirs
Expert waterproofing from roofs to foundations
Bitumen waterproofing for slab roofs and cement or gravel dams
Preventative maintenance with regular inspections and upkeep

Agriculture and game farming dominate our dam and tank work, but mines, estates, schools, warehouses and small commercial buildings use our waterproofing and maintenance services too. Whether you are a first-time smallholder or a mine planning containment upgrades, you get the same technical honesty on liner grade and realistic timelines.

We source HDPE, PVC, bitumen membranes and galvanised steel from established suppliers. Qualifying materials may carry a supplier-backed material warranty where stated in the project quotation, subject to the supplier’s terms. Our aim is dams that hold water and roofs that stay dry long after sign-off.

/about-us-waterproofing-company/.mobileVisibleText: Home / About Us More than 30 years of combined team experience About Damtech Damtech provides dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage solutions for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties across South Africa. Request a Quote Contact Damtech Damtech provides dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage solutions for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties across South Africa. We install HDPE and PVC dam linings on farms and mines, build corrugated steel reservoirs, and apply bitumen waterproofing on roofs and foundations, always with an emphasis on workmanship you can inspect, not promises you cannot keep. Who Are We? We are Damtech — specialists in earth dam linings, waterproofing and steel water storage tanks. The Damtech team brings more than 30 years of combined experience across dam linings, waterproofing and water-storage projects. We deliver practical solutions that safeguard your investment and support long-term performance. Andre de Lange — Owner Andre has worked in dam lining, waterproofing and water-storage installations since the late 1990s. His experience includes HDPE, PVC, bitumen, steel tanks and concrete roofs across South Africa. At Damtech, he is responsible for site assessment, project supervision, installation, quality checks and client coordination. Our Mission To provide top-tier waterproofing and lining solutions that stand the test of time. We strive to exceed our clients' expectations by offering reliable, effective and tailored services — whether you need advanced earth dam linings for large-scale dams or expert waterproofing for roofs and foundations. Digital platform built by Koppie Systems . Practical dam linings, waterproofing and water storage solutions. WHY DAMTECH Experience You Can Trust Damtech delivers practical dam linings, waterproofing and water storage solutions with a focus on long-term leak prevention and reliable workmanship. Locally Owned Proudly based in South Africa, with practical understanding of local site conditions, climate and client requirements. Practical Contractor Experience Decades of experience in dam linings, waterproofing, reservoir lining and water storage for farms, mines and commercial sites. Serving South Africa Dam linings, steel water tanks and waterproofing projects for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties nationwide. Trusted by Property Owners Practical solutions for agricultural, mining, estate and commercial water storage with supplier-backed materials where applicable. Three Decades of Lining and Waterproofing Experience Our teams have lined irrigation dams in the Western Cape, built steel tanks for Mpumalanga citrus farms, and repaired torch-on roofs on Gauteng commercial stores. That range helps us understand regional soils, rainfall patterns and the pressure load-shedding puts on borehole and pumping schedules, which shapes how we specify liners and tank sizes. How We Approach Every Project We listen first: what water you need to store, how you use it, and what has failed before. Then we recommend materials and thicknesses that fit the site, not whatever is cheapest to freight. Installation crews prepare substrates properly, weld and anchor to spec, and leave you with maintenance guidance. After handover we are still a phone call away for inspections, patches and expansions. OUR SERVICES What We Do Dam linings, steel water tanks and waterproofing for farms, mines and commercial properties. Earth Dam Linings HDPE, PVC and bitumen torch-on lining for agricultural farm dams, mining ponds and irrigation storage nationwide. Dam linings Steel Water Tanks Corrugated galvanised reservoirs from 11 kL to 500 kL+ with PVC lining, columns and optional roofs. Steel water tanks Waterproofing Bitumen torch-on and maintenance for roofs, foundations and retaining structures on farms and commercial buildings. Waterproofing WHAT WE DELIVER Specialised Services Steel water storage tanks with custom sizes, roofs and support columns HDPE geomembrane linings for large gravel and farm dams PVC linings for ponds and zinc reservoirs Expert waterproofing from roofs to foundations Bitumen waterproofing for slab roofs and cement or gravel dams Preventative maintenance with regular inspections and upkeep Sectors We Serve Agriculture and game farming dominate our dam and tank work, but mines, estates, schools, warehouses and small commercial buildings use our waterproofing and maintenance services too. Whether you are a first-time smallholder or a mine planning containment upgrades, you get the same technical honesty on liner grade and realistic timelines. Quality Materials and Accountable Installation We source HDPE, PVC, bitumen membranes and galvanised steel from established suppliers. Qualifying materials may carry a supplier-backed material warranty where stated in the project quotation, subject to the supplier’s terms. Our aim is dams that hold water and roofs that stay dry long after sign-off. Agricultural Water Storage
Plan farm water security with lined earth dams, steel reservoirs and maintenance — integrated storage for irrigation, livestock and borehole backup.

Single-dam thinking leaves farms exposed. A typical resilient layout combines catchment storage in a lined earth dam, pressurised or clean water in a steel tank near the homestead, and borehole pumping timed around load-shedding. Agricultural water storage is not only about volume — it is about where water sits in the system when pivots start, when calving season peaks, and when municipal supply throttles back.
LOCAL CONDITIONS

Rainfall region dictates strategy. Summer-rainfall grain farms fill between October and January and spend stored water through May. Winter-rainfall producers must retain nearly a year of irrigation need from three wet months. Bushveld game farms hold permanent pools for wildlife through six dry months. Each pattern changes how much storage, what liner type, and whether roofs on steel tanks are worth the capital.
SITE FACTORS

Catchment soils determine natural yield and seepage. Sandy catchments fill quickly but seep without HDPE. Clay catchments hold better unlined but still fail on fissured beds. Integrated planning looks at both the dam basin and the tank pad — steel tanks need level compacted bases independent of dam geology.
WATER USE

Storage must match peak daily irrigation demand, not average rainfall. A pivot that needs a fixed megalitre per day cannot run from a dam that seeped half its winter fill before October. Borehole-linked systems need storage sized for nights of pumping when power is available. Packhouses and tunnels often need a smaller clean reserve isolated from muddy farm dam water.
SECTORS

Fruit, wine, sugar, grain, livestock and game operations all use different withdrawal rates but share the need for predictable storage. Agribusiness with multiple titles may centralise storage in one lined dam and distribute via pipelines. Emerging farmers consolidating smallholdings often upgrade one shared dam before adding tanks at each homestead.
STORAGE

Damtech helps clients sequence projects: line the primary dam first, add steel backup where drinking or household security matters, waterproof cement reservoirs feeding tunnels, and maintain roofs before summer leaks ruin stored hay. Our regional pages cover Western Cape, Limpopo and Gauteng specifics, and our projects page shows completed farm and industrial work.

FAQ
Large catchments favour lined earth dams. Steel tanks suit smaller volumes, elevated sites or phased expansion. Many farms line the main dam first, then add tanks near critical uses.
Yes. We quote integrated scopes or phased work — dam lining now, tanks when civils are ready.
Tanks store water pumped when power is available, so irrigation or stock lines can draw while borehole pumps are offline.
We install physical storage. Licensing and entitlement remain with your water consultant or authority — we align capacity with the storage you are permitted to develop.

Each pattern changes how much storage, what liner type, and whether roofs on steel tanks are worth the capital. SITE FACTORS Soils & Ground Conditions Catchment soils determine natural yield and seepage. Sandy catchments fill quickly but seep without HDPE. Clay catchments hold better unlined but still fail on fissured beds. Integrated planning looks at both the dam basin and the tank pad — steel tanks need level compacted bases independent of dam geology. A pivot that needs a fixed megalitre per day cannot run from a dam that seeped half its winter fill before October. Borehole-linked systems need storage sized for nights of pumping when power is available. Packhouses and tunnels often need a smaller clean reserve isolated from muddy farm dam water. Agribusiness with multiple titles may centralise storage in one lined dam and distribute via pipelines. Emerging farmers consolidating smallholdings often upgrade one shared dam before adding tanks at each homestead. /Assessing the Environmental Impact of Different Dam Lining Materials on South African Farmland
By Andre de Lange·15 November 2025

Water storage is a critical part of farming and land management in South Africa. Reliable dams and reservoirs provide water for livestock, irrigation, household use, and fire protection. However, the materials used to line these dams can influence not only the water retention but also the health of the surrounding soil, ecosystems, and water quality. Making informed choices about dam lining materials helps ensure sustainable farm management that supports both productivity and environmental stewardship.
The lining material in a dam serves to reduce water loss through seepage and erosion. But its impact goes beyond water retention:
Soil health: Some linings can affect the soil structure and microbial communities around the dam.
Water quality: Materials can leach substances into the water or affect the growth of algae and bacteria.
Local ecosystems: The lining can influence habitats for plants, insects, and animals.
Choosing the right lining material means balancing durability, cost, and environmental impact to support sustainable farming.
Several lining options are popular for farm dams and reservoirs. Each has different environmental considerations.
Traditionally, many farm dams rely on natural clay or compacted soil to reduce seepage.
Environmental pros: Natural, biodegradable, and generally compatible with local soil ecosystems.
Environmental cons: Can crack when dry, leading to seepage and sediment loss; may require re-compaction or resealing over time.
Impact on soil and water: Usually minimal chemical impact; however, poor compaction can lead to erosion and sediment entering water.
Plastic liners are widely used for their impermeability and ease of installation.
Environmental pros: Highly effective at preventing seepage, protecting water supplies.
Environmental cons: Made from non-biodegradable materials derived from fossil fuels; risk of microplastic contamination if damaged.
Impact on soil and water: Potential chemical additives can leach; liners can create barriers affecting soil moisture and earthworm activity.
These combine fabrics with rubber or plastic layers to increase strength and durability.
Environmental pros: Durable with good resistance to UV and punctures; designed to limit seepage.
Environmental cons: Similar concerns to plastic liners regarding biodegradability and chemical leaching.
Impact on soil and water: May alter natural soil-water interactions beneath the liner.
Corrugated steel reservoirs often use steel panels combined with waterproof linings to form above-ground or partially buried water tanks.
Environmental pros: Recyclable materials, robust construction reduces risk of leakage and contamination.
Environmental cons: Requires protective coatings to prevent rust; manufacturing impact depends on steel sourcing and processing.
Impact on soil and water: Steel and coatings must be environmentally safe to prevent water contamination; minimal soil disturbance once installed.
Healthy soil supports plant growth and ecosystem functions. Dam linings can influence soil properties in the following ways:

Natural linings like clay integrate with the soil and often maintain natural porosity. Plastic or composite liners create barriers that can disrupt natural water infiltration and gas exchange, potentially leading to soil compaction or reduced microbial activity near the dam.

Soil microbes thrive in balanced moisture and nutrient conditions. Synthetic liners can change moisture dynamics, sometimes reducing microbial diversity. Non-toxic, natural linings tend to support healthier microbial ecosystems.
Some liner materials may leach chemicals or microplastics into surrounding soil, especially if damaged. This can affect soil organisms and plant roots.
Dams are part of the broader farm ecosystem, often supporting wildlife and native vegetation.
Natural or clay-lined dams generally support more edge vegetation and encourage visits from birds, insects, and amphibians.
Synthetic liners can limit natural seepage, which may reduce moisture availability for nearby plants.
Steel reservoirs, being above ground or contained, typically have less interaction with the surrounding soil but reduce habitat availability around the structure.
Farmers should consider how dam design and lining choices fit into their broader land management and conservation goals.
Water stored in dams is used for livestock, irrigation, and sometimes household use, so maintaining quality is essential.
Effective liners reduce seepage that can carry nutrients and sediments into groundwater or downstream ecosystems. This helps maintain water clarity and reduce eutrophication risks.

Plastic liners may leach additives or plasticizers, especially under UV exposure or temperature fluctuations. Steel reservoirs with appropriate coatings avoid rust contamination but need regular inspection.

Some materials can encourage or inhibit algae growth. For example, dark liners absorb heat, potentially increasing water temperature and algae blooms. Conversely, liners that limit nutrient entry can reduce algae.
Assess local soil and climate: Clay linings may work well in areas with sufficient natural clay content and moderate climate.
Consider dam use and water needs: High-value water uses may justify more durable synthetic liners with proper environmental safeguards.
Evaluate longevity and maintenance: Natural linings may need more upkeep; synthetic liners or steel reservoirs offer longer-term solutions but require environmental monitoring.
Minimise environmental disturbance during installation: Avoid unnecessary clearing of vegetation and soil compaction.
Plan for end-of-life disposal or recycling: Choose materials that can be recycled or safely disposed of.
Corrugated steel reservoirs combined with quality linings offer a practical solution for farmers needing durable, leak-resistant water storage. These systems are particularly suitable when:
Reliable water storage with minimal seepage is essential.
Space or soil conditions limit the feasibility of traditional earth dams.
Quick installation and ease of maintenance are priorities.
A robust structure is needed to protect against damage from animals, machinery, or weather.

While steel reservoirs may have a different environmental footprint compared to natural earth dams, their recyclability and controlled water quality can be advantages in sustainable farm water management.

Choosing the right dam lining material involves balancing environmental impact with functional needs. Natural clay linings support soil health and ecosystems but may require more maintenance. Synthetic liners and steel reservoirs provide excellent water retention and durability but come with considerations around material sourcing, potential contamination, and soil interactions.
By understanding how different materials influence soil, water, and ecosystems, South African farmers can make informed decisions that promote sustainable agriculture and long-term farm resilience.
If you’d like help sizing a reservoir or choosing a lining, contact Damtech through the quote form on our website.
We supply, line and repair corrugated steel reservoirs — including bitumen and HDPE lining options.

DAMTECH CALCULATORS
Use these practical tools to estimate dam lining area, waterproofing material, steel water tank sizing and annual water storage requirements before requesting a quote.

Use Damtech's planning calculators to estimate dam lining area, dam liner material quantities, steel water tank sizing, waterproofing area, irrigation water requirements, rainwater harvesting potential and water storage needs across South Africa. These tools help farms, mines, game lodges and commercial properties prepare dimensions and demand figures before requesting a dam lining quote.

The dam lining area calculator helps you estimate geomembrane material for earth dams, ponds and reservoirs. Enter top and bottom dimensions, depth and side slope to plan HDPE or PVC dam liner material before a site inspection. Overlap, anchor trench and wastage allowances are applied automatically as Damtech planning defaults.

The steel water tank size calculator estimates corrugated steel reservoir capacity from daily water use, backup storage days and a safety factor — useful when sizing farm, lodge or commercial water storage. Compare the result with Damtech’s fixed-price 20 000L, 50 000L and 100 000L supply-only kits.

Plan annual farm water demand, land-size based requirements and crop irrigation needs with our annual water requirement, water by land size and irrigation water requirement calculators. The rainwater harvesting calculator estimates catchment yield for tank or lined dam storage planning.

Use the waterproofing area calculator to estimate bitumen or torch-on material for roofs, reservoirs, channels and water-retaining structures. Upstands are entered on the form; overlap and wastage allowances are applied automatically.
SELECT A TOOL

Select a dam lining calculator, water storage tool or waterproofing estimator based on your project. Each tool provides preliminary planning estimates for farms, mines and properties across South Africa.

GUIDANCE
These calculators provide early planning estimates only. They help you prepare dimensions, water demand and material areas before requesting a dam lining quote or site inspection from Damtech.

Final material quantities depend on site inspection, slopes, anchor trenches, overlaps, waste, access and supplier specifications. Irrigation and water requirement values depend on rainfall, crop type, soil, system efficiency and seasonal demand.

Damtech can confirm requirements during quote and site inspection. For accurate dam liner material estimates, steel water tank sizing or waterproofing area calculations, send us your site photos and dimensions.
Explore our dam lining services, HDPE dam lining and steel water tanks for more detail on Damtech solutions.

These calculators provide preliminary planning estimates only. Final material quantities, water storage requirements and installation recommendations must be confirmed by Damtech after reviewing site dimensions, site conditions, access, material specifications and project requirements.
Calculator results are not engineering designs, legal water-use approvals or final quotations.
FAQ
Common questions about dam lining calculators, water storage estimates and quote preparation.
Can I use the dam lining calculator for a final quote?
No. It provides a preliminary estimate only. Final material quantities depend on site dimensions, slopes, anchor trenches, overlap, wastage, access and material specifications.
What measurements do I need for a dam lining estimate?

Collect the top length and width, bottom length and width, depth and side slope. Freeboard can be adjusted if needed. Overlap, anchor trench and wastage allowances are applied automatically as Damtech planning defaults.
Can the calculator estimate water requirements for a farm?

Yes, the page includes planning calculators for annual water demand, land-size based water requirements and irrigation water requirements. Final values depend on crop type, rainfall, soil conditions and irrigation efficiency.
Can Damtech help if my dam is already leaking?
Yes. Use the leaking dam repair assessment tool to prepare basic information, then request a site-specific inspection or quote.
Are calculator results engineering designs?
No. The calculators provide planning estimates only and do not replace engineering design, water-use approval, supplier specifications or a formal Damtech quotation.

/Choosing the Best Dam Lining Solutions to Prevent Seepage in Sandy and Clay Soils Common in South African Farmlands
By Andre de Lange·17 November 2025

Water is the lifeblood of any farm or rural property, especially in South Africa where rainfall can be unpredictable and droughts are a serious concern. Ensuring your dam or reservoir retains as much water as possible is critical for livestock, irrigation, and household use. One of the biggest challenges faced by farmers and landowners is seepage — the slow loss of water through the soil beneath and around dams.

In this guide, we’ll explore how to select the best dam lining solutions specifically tailored to the common soil types found on South African farmlands: sandy and clay soils. We’ll cover the pros and cons of traditional clay liners, modern HDPE liners, and innovative composite lining systems. By understanding these options, you can improve water retention, reduce costly maintenance, and protect your investment in water infrastructure.

Before choosing a lining solution, it’s essential to understand the soil conditions where your dam is located. South African farmlands typically have two major soil types relevant to dam construction:
Characteristics: Coarse texture, large particles, high permeability
Seepage Risk: High — water easily drains through sandy soils, leading to significant seepage losses
Challenges: Difficult to compact; prone to erosion and instability around dam edges
Characteristics: Fine particles, low permeability, high plasticity
Seepage Risk: Low to moderate — clay naturally restricts water flow, but cracks can develop when dry
Challenges: Can shrink and crack in dry conditions, causing seepage paths; may be difficult to source suitable clay locally
Soil classification and mapping resources can help you identify the specific soil type on your property, which is the first step toward choosing the right dam lining.
Traditional clay liners use compacted clay material excavated or imported to form a natural barrier that limits water seepage.
Advantages:
Natural and environmentally friendly
Relatively low cost if suitable clay is available onsite
Good water retention when properly installed and maintained
Disadvantages:
Requires careful compaction and moisture control during installation
Vulnerable to cracking during dry spells, leading to seepage
Limited availability of high-quality clay in some regions
Higher maintenance to repair cracks or erosion

Clay liners can be effective in areas where quality clay is readily accessible and where regular maintenance is feasible. However, their performance can vary widely depending on local conditions and installation expertise.
HDPE liners are synthetic plastic sheets engineered specifically for water containment. They have become a popular choice for dam lining due to their durability and low permeability.
Extremely low permeability — virtually eliminates seepage
Highly resistant to UV exposure, chemicals, and punctures
Flexible and adaptable to uneven ground surfaces
Long lifespan with minimal maintenance
Higher upfront material and installation costs compared to clay
Requires skilled installation to ensure seams are properly welded
Can be damaged by sharp objects or livestock if not protected

HDPE liners are particularly well-suited to sandy soils where natural seepage is high and where a reliable, low-maintenance water barrier is desired. They are also valuable for dams that serve critical water needs or are difficult to maintain regularly.
Composite liners combine synthetic materials such as HDPE or PVC with natural materials like clay or geotextiles to create a multi-layered barrier.
Combines strength and flexibility of synthetic liners with the natural sealing properties of clay
Can reduce costs compared to full synthetic liners
Improved protection against punctures and damage
More complex installation processes
May require specialized design and engineering
Not as widely available or standardized as pure clay or HDPE liners
Composite liners can be a practical choice for landowners looking to balance cost with performance, especially when partial site conditions favor different materials.
Selecting the best lining depends on several factors, including soil type, budget, dam size, intended use, and maintenance capacity. Here are key considerations to guide your decision:
Perform a soil test or consult local agricultural extension services to confirm soil type
Check for the availability of quality clay on or near your property
Evaluate the dam’s shape, depth, and substrate stability
How much water do you need to store?
What is the primary use: livestock, irrigation, household consumption, or game?
Do you require a lining that requires minimal maintenance?
Is skilled labor available locally for liner installation?
Can you protect the liner from damage by animals or machinery?
Are you prepared for periodic inspections and repairs?
Compare the upfront and ongoing costs of each lining type
Factor in the expected lifespan and replacement intervals
Consider the cost of water loss due to seepage if no lining or an inadequate lining is used

In many cases, especially when constructing new reservoirs or upgrading existing dams, combining robust structures like corrugated steel reservoirs with high-quality linings such as HDPE offers a reliable solution. Corrugated steel reservoirs provide strong, durable containment that resists environmental wear, while HDPE linings ensure a nearly impermeable barrier to seepage.
These systems are particularly well-suited for:
Areas with sandy soils where natural seepage is a major problem
Locations where clay is scarce or unsuitable for lining
Farms requiring long-term, low-maintenance water storage
Situations where water quality and retention are critical for livestock or irrigation

While the initial investment may be higher than traditional earth dams, the durability and water savings often justify the cost over time. Additionally, professional installation and expert liner selection help maximise the lifespan of your reservoir.
Department of Water and Sanitation – Water Infrastructure Projects
Agricultural Research Council – Soil and Water Management
International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD) – Best Practices and Guidelines

Preventing seepage in dams on sandy and clay soils requires understanding your site’s unique conditions and carefully selecting a lining that balances cost, durability, and maintenance. While traditional clay liners remain an option in some areas, modern HDPE liners and composite systems offer superior performance and peace of mind for many South African landowners.
Combining these linings with reliable structures like corrugated steel reservoirs can further enhance water security on your farm or property.

If you’d like help sizing a reservoir or choosing a lining, contact Damtech through the quote form on our website. Our expertise in corrugated steel reservoirs, HDPE linings, and leak repair services can guide you to the best solution for your water storage needs.
We supply, line and repair corrugated steel reservoirs — including bitumen and HDPE lining options.

/Cost-Benefit Analysis of Upgrading to Corrugated Steel Reservoirs for Long-Term Farm Water Security
By Andre de Lange·18 November 2025

Water security is a critical concern for South African farmers and landowners, especially given the country’s recurring droughts and variable rainfall patterns. Reliable water storage is essential for sustaining livestock, game, irrigation systems, household needs, and even fire protection. Upgrading to corrugated steel reservoirs can be a strategic investment for long-term water security. This article provides a detailed cost-benefit analysis to help you evaluate whether switching to corrugated steel reservoirs makes sense for your farm.

Corrugated steel reservoirs are water storage tanks made from galvanized or coated steel sheets shaped into corrugations for extra strength. These reservoirs are often lined with durable materials to prevent leaks and contamination.
Durability: Resistant to rust, UV damage, and physical impact.
Modularity: Available in various sizes and can be expanded or relocated.
Ease of Installation: Faster to install than concrete or earth dams.
Low Maintenance: Requires less upkeep compared to traditional dams or earth reservoirs.
When considering upgrading to a corrugated steel reservoir, it helps to break down the costs into initial investment and ongoing expenses.
Purchase Price: The upfront cost depends on the size and lining options chosen.
Installation: Includes site preparation, assembly, and lining installation.
Site Work: May involve earthworks or grading to ensure stable placement.
Maintenance: Generally low. Routine inspections and occasional cleaning are typical.
Repairs: Lining repairs might be needed after many years, but steel structure repairs are rare.
Water Treatment: If required, depends on water use but is separate from reservoir costs.

Corrugated steel reservoirs are designed to withstand harsh South African weather conditions, including intense sun, wind, and fluctuating temperatures. Their galvanized coating protects against rust, and when combined with quality linings, these reservoirs can last for decades with minimal degradation.

Compared to earth dams or plastic tanks, steel reservoirs require less frequent maintenance. They don’t suffer from liner punctures as easily as plastic options and are less prone to leaks caused by animal activity or shifting ground.

During droughts, reliable water storage becomes even more crucial. Corrugated steel reservoirs can be sized appropriately to capture and store maximum rainfall and surface runoff, securing water availability for livestock and crops. Their sealed design also reduces evaporation compared to open earth dams.

Because these reservoirs are modular and portable, you can install them in locations best suited for water catchment or close to points of use, reducing water loss in transportation and enhancing efficiency.
Properly lined steel reservoirs can prevent contamination from soil and debris, helping maintain better water quality for sensitive uses like household consumption or irrigation.

The initial investment in a corrugated steel reservoir may be higher than some alternatives like earth dams, but the reduced maintenance and longer lifespan often offset these costs. Consider the following financial factors:
Maintenance Savings: Less frequent repairs and cleaning reduce labour and material expenses over time.
Water Loss Reduction: Lower evaporation and leakage mean less water needs to be sourced or pumped, saving on operational costs.
Resilience to Drought: Securing water availability can protect your farm’s productivity and income during dry spells, an indirect but significant financial benefit.
Depreciation and Longevity: A well-maintained steel reservoir can serve a farm for 20 years or more, spreading costs over a longer period than plastic tanks.
Corrugated steel reservoirs are suitable for a variety of farm water needs, including:
Cattle and Livestock: Reliable drinking water supply in remote paddocks.
Game Farming: Secure watering points that can be moved as grazing patterns change.
Irrigation: Storage tanks close to fields reduce pumping and distribution costs.
Household Water Supply: Clean, lined tanks protect water quality for domestic use.
Fire Protection: Large capacity tanks provide emergency water reserves.
Choosing a corrugated steel reservoir and lining solution is particularly worthwhile when:
You need a durable, long-term water storage solution that can withstand harsh environmental conditions.
Your farm experiences frequent droughts or irregular rainfall, making reliable water storage critical.
Maintenance resources and labour availability are limited, and you want to reduce ongoing upkeep.
You require flexibility in size and location, such as for rotational grazing or changing irrigation needs.
You want to improve water quality by preventing contamination and leakage.
While upfront costs may be higher than some alternatives, the practical benefits and cost savings over time often justify the investment for serious water security planning.

Upgrading to corrugated steel reservoirs offers South African farmers a practical, durable, and cost-effective method to safeguard water supplies for livestock, irrigation, household use, and fire protection. By carefully evaluating the initial and ongoing costs alongside the operational benefits, you can make an informed decision that supports your farm’s resilience through drought and changing climate conditions.
If you’d like help sizing a reservoir or choosing a lining, contact Damtech through the quote form on our website.
We supply, line and repair corrugated steel reservoirs — including bitumen and HDPE lining options.

/Critical Water Storage Tips to Overcome Borehole Water Shortages During South African Droughts
By Andre de Lange·19 November 2025

Water scarcity is a pressing challenge for many South African farmers, especially during prolonged droughts. Boreholes, a common water source on farms, often suffer from reduced yields or even run dry when rainfall is low. Managing and optimising water storage can make the difference between maintaining your livestock, crops, and household needs or facing severe water stress. In this article, we explore practical strategies to identify borehole water shortages, effective water storage solutions, and how integrating farm dams with boreholes can secure your irrigation needs throughout dry spells.

Borehole water shortages occur when the groundwater supply feeding the borehole decreases or becomes insufficient for your farm’s demands. Understanding the signs early can help you take proactive steps.
Reduced flow rate: Noticeably less water coming from taps or pumps than usual.
Longer pump run times: Pumps working harder or running more frequently without delivering adequate water.
Changes in water quality: Increased turbidity, saltiness, or unusual tastes, which can indicate stressed aquifers.
Lower water levels in borehole: Measured drops in static water level inside the borehole casing.
Regular monitoring of borehole performance helps detect shortages early. The South African Weather Service provides drought alerts and rainfall data that can assist in planning for water shortages.
Extended droughts: Reduced rainfall leads to lower groundwater recharge.
Over-extraction: Drawing more water than the aquifer can replenish.
Seasonal fluctuations: Natural changes in water table levels throughout the year.
Geological factors: Some aquifers have limited storage capacity or slow recharge rates.

When borehole output is unreliable, having adequate water storage becomes essential to keep your farm running smoothly. Here are practical options and tips to improve your water storage capacity and efficiency.

Durable and versatile, corrugated steel reservoirs are widely used in South Africa for storing large volumes of water. They are quick to assemble, scalable, and suitable for various water uses—from livestock to irrigation to domestic needs.
Advantages: Long lifespan, resistant to pests, can be lined to prevent leaks.
Considerations: Must be installed on stable ground, and lined properly to prevent contamination or seepage.

Traditional earth dams can lose water through seepage and evaporation, especially in hot climates. Lining these dams with high-density polyethylene (HDPE) can drastically reduce losses and improve water retention.
Benefits of HDPE lining: Minimises seepage, reduces evaporation, and extends dam lifespan.
Environmental impact: Protects soil and groundwater quality by preventing contamination.
For more information on dam lining, you can visit the Damtech Dam Linings page.
Maximise rainfall capture by installing gutters and channels directing water into storage tanks or dams. Even small volumes collected during rains can supplement borehole water during shortages.
Use sediment filters to keep harvested water clean.
Consider covered tanks to reduce evaporation.
Integrate rainwater harvesting with existing reservoirs to increase total available water.
Water losses through leaks in reservoirs, pipelines, or dams can be significant. Routine inspections and timely repairs preserve precious water resources.
Inspect corrugated steel reservoirs for corrosion or joint weaknesses.
Use professional leak repair services to maintain reservoir integrity.
Check dam walls and linings for punctures or damage.
Damtech offers expert Leak Repair Services tailored for farm reservoirs and dams.
Rather than relying solely on boreholes, combining multiple water sources can build resilience against droughts. Here’s how integrating boreholes with farm dams can improve water security:
Buffer against shortages: Dams store surface runoff and rainwater, reducing pressure on boreholes.
Flexible irrigation scheduling: Use dam water during low borehole yields.
Reduced pump wear: Less frequent borehole pumping extends equipment lifespan.
Improved livestock watering: Multiple sources ensure constant supply.
Design your farm dam size and lining with future irrigation needs in mind.
Install pumps and piping systems that can draw from both sources.
Monitor water levels in both boreholes and dams regularly.
Consider water quality differences and treat accordingly.
Corrugated steel reservoirs combined with HDPE linings offer a practical, durable solution for many South African farmers facing borehole water shortages. They are especially suitable when:
You need a scalable, long-lasting water storage solution that can be adapted to your farm’s changing needs.
Your existing earth dams suffer from seepage or contamination issues and require lining to improve water retention and quality.
You want a low-maintenance reservoir option resistant to rodents and environmental wear.
Quick installation is needed to respond to urgent water storage demands during drought periods.
While not the sole solution, these reservoirs and linings complement boreholes effectively, increasing your overall water security and helping manage borehole water shortages more confidently.
For more detailed information on our water storage products and services, see our Damtech website.

South African farmers must face the reality of borehole water shortages during droughts with smart water management strategies. By identifying shortages early, investing in reliable storage solutions like corrugated steel reservoirs and HDPE-lined dams, and integrating various water sources, you can safeguard your farm’s productivity and resilience.

If you’d like help sizing a reservoir or choosing a lining, contact Damtech through the quote form on our website. Our team understands local conditions and can support you in making the best water storage decisions for your farm.
We supply, line and repair corrugated steel reservoirs — including bitumen and HDPE lining options.

Corrugated steel reservoirs combined with HDPE linings offer a practical, durable solution for many South African farmers facing borehole water shortages. They are especially suitable when: You need a scalable, long-lasting water storage solution that can be adapted to your farm’s changing needs. Your existing earth dams suffer from seepage or contamination issues and require lining to improve water retention and quality. You want a low-maintenance reservoir option resistant to rodents and environmental wear. Quick installation is needed to respond to urgent water storage demands during drought periods. While not the sole solution, these reservoirs and linings complement boreholes effectively, increasing your overall water security and helping manage borehole water shortages more confidently. For more detailed information on our water storage products and services, see our Damtech website . Final Thoughts South African farmers must face the reality of borehole water shortages during droughts with smart water management strategies. By identifying shortages early, investing in reliable storage solutions like corrugated steel reservoirs and HDPE-lined dams, and integrating various water sources, you can safeguard your farm’s productivity and resilience. If you’d like help sizing a reservoir or choosing a lining, contact Damtech through the quote form on our website. Our team understands local conditions and can support you in making the best water storage decisions for your farm. “` Need help with a steel reservoir or tank? Transparent quoting · No hidden shortcuts
Dam lining cost depends on liner type, dam size, site access and preparation — not a single price per square metre. Here is what drives your quote.
DAM LINING COST GUIDANCE

Clients often ask for a ballpark dam lining price before sharing dam dimensions or photos. An accurate quote requires an understanding of surface area, liner grade, subgrade condition, access for equipment and whether outlets and anchor trenches need rework. Damtech provides tailored quotes after assessment; this page explains the factors so you know what to prepare.
Quote based on site-specific assessment
Material matched to use — not cheapest roll
Preparation scope included in writing
Thickness options explained (1–2 mm HDPE)•Travel and mobilisation quoted upfront•No generic price-per-m² figures that can mislead budgets
WHY IT MATTERS
Thickness options explained (1–2 mm HDPE)
Travel and mobilisation quoted upfront
No generic price-per-m² figures that can mislead budgets
TECHNICAL DETAIL
Primary drivers
Area, liner type, thickness, access
HDPE
Typically specified 1–2 mm for farm dams
PVC
550–850 gsm for ponds and tanks
Extras
Geotextile, outlets, dewatering, rock fill
Next step
Free quote with photos or site visit

Surface area is the starting point, but steep batters, rocky subgrades, remote access and existing water in the dam all change crew days and material waste. Outlet penetrations, anchor trenches and crest protection add detail work beyond plain field sheet. Labour and freight to a remote site in Limpopo will differ from a Gauteng farm 40 km from Pretoria.

HDPE material can cost more per roll, but it is often chosen for large dams for its UV resistance, longevity and low seepage. PVC can lower material cost on small ponds and tank linings where rolls are manageable. Bitumen torch-on is priced on prepared concrete area and detail complexity — not comparable directly to m² HDPE on earth.

A smooth, compacted subgrade with geotextile costs less to line than a rocky batter that needs padding and hand finishing. Dewatering, silt removal and crest regrading are often the scope items left out of low quotes, which then cause cost overruns mid-project.

Narrow farm roads, limited loader or crane reach for heavy liner rolls, and steep batters slow production compared with gently sloped dams that have good perimeter access. Anchor trenches at the crest must be specified and included; shallow trenches are a common reason liners pull loose under wind uplift or load.

Under-specified thickness, skipped geotextile, poor welding and missing outlet boots can cause leaks within a few seasons, after which relining costs more than doing the job properly once. We quote for inspectable workmanship, not the lowest m² figure on paper.

Send dam length and width (or surface m²), photos of batters and crest, intended use, province and whether the dam holds water now. Use our quote form or call us, and we will confirm the next steps: a site visit or a detailed estimate.
HOW IT WORKS
From your first enquiry to final handover, Damtech keeps the process clear, practical and hassle-free.
Tell us what you need, including dam linings, waterproofing, steel water tanks, maintenance or repair.
No obligation. No pressure.
We assess the application, site conditions and practical requirements for your project.
Thorough. Practical. Honest.
We recommend a suitable material, system and installation approach for your site.
Clear recommendations.
Our team delivers the agreed service with clear communication and practical workmanship.
On time. On standard.
OUR PROJECTS
Quality materials, expert installation and practical solutions for dam linings, waterproofing and water storage.

Three earth dams at a North West game lodge were lined with 1 mm HDPE geomembrane, covering a combined area of 2,098 m².

13,360 m² HDPE dam liner supply and installation for farm water storage.
Large-scale HDPE earth dam lining in the Stellenbosch wine and agricultural district — 13,360 m² installed for reliable farm water storage.

HDPE dam lining
3,400 m² HDPE liner installation for agricultural water storage.
Grabouw farm dam lined with 3,400 m² HDPE to protect irrigation reserves in the Western Cape fruit belt.
Hoedspruit, Limpopo
Limpopo
Bitumen torch-on dam lining
550 m² bitumen torch-on lining for cement / structured dam waterproofing.
Hoedspruit structured dam waterproofed with 550 m² bitumen torch-on lining for Lowveld water storage.
Centurion, Gauteng
Gauteng
1,200 m² HDPE dam liner for farm water storage in the Centurion / Pretoria corridor.
Centurion farm dam lined with 1,200 m² HDPE to protect irrigation water in Gauteng.
Tzaneen, Limpopo
Concrete dam waterproofing

Torch-on bitumen waterproofing for a round concrete dam with an 18 m diameter. Approximately 255 m² circular base footprint, calculated from the 18 m diameter. This is a geometric base-area estimate — not the measured installed membrane quantity. Installed membrane area is higher once walls are included — roughly +130 m² if the wall is 2.3 m high all around (π × 18 m × 2.3 m), plus overlaps, detailing and waste.

Practical repair for leaking farm dams, failed geomembrane liners and water storage systems — assessed on site before we recommend patch, overlay or full reline.

Repair types

First step

Wet patches below the wall, an unexplained drop in water level after rain, or muddy seepage on batters often point to liner failure or a porous subgrade, not evaporation alone. On lined dams, bubbles under the membrane, exposed edges at the crest and animal damage at drinking points are common culprits. Steel and concrete reservoirs may leak at panel joints, rusted outlets or failed internal PVC lining.
Early inspection is usually cheaper than emergency relining during peak irrigation. Log water levels over several still days without inflow or use to help separate evaporation from seepage.

UV embrittlement of exposed crest rolls, hoof traffic on unprotected batters, rocky subgrades without geotextile and poor seam welding during the original installation are frequent causes of failure on HDPE systems. PVC ponds fail at folds and penetrations. Torch-on membranes delaminate when moisture was trapped beneath the substrate or flashings were omitted at parapets.

Localised punctures on sound HDPE are often patch-welded after the area is cleaned and dried. Widespread UV cracking, multiple seam failures or subgrade collapse usually justify full relining after the embankment is stabilised. We explain trade-offs clearly so you can budget for the right scope.

Patch repairs use compatible HDPE sheet and extrusion or hot-air welding, with vacuum or air-pressure testing on critical seams where practical. Full relines follow the same preparation standards as new installs: dewatering, subgrade repair, geotextile where needed, anchor trenches and outlet boots detailed to spec.

Annual crest walks, outlet checks and silt management help extend liner life. We offer inspection visits before planting or calving seasons and document findings with photos for insurance or farm records.

/Farm Dam Leak Diagnosis and Repair Guide for South Africa
By Andre de Lange·1 December 2025

Leaks in a farm dam or reservoir rarely announce themselves with a single dramatic failure. More often they show as a water level that drops faster than evaporation, a wet patch on the embankment toe, or a soft spot where liner has pulled away from the crest. This guide is about diagnosis and assessment — how to find a leak, how to judge how serious it is, and which temporary measures are reasonable before a specialist arrives.
If you already know you need a contractor on site, have Damtech assess a leaking dam rather than treating this article as a substitute for a site inspection.

Every megalitre lost to seepage is water that will not reach livestock, pivots or game through a dry month. Small leaks also tend to widen: embankment fines migrate, liner tears grow under UV and stock traffic, and corroded fittings fail more quickly once water tracks through the panel. Early detection limits:
Shortfalls during dry seasons when borehole pumping is already expensive
Secondary damage — embankment erosion, undermined tank pads, muddy approaches
Contamination risk where seepage paths connect dirty runoff to stored water
The chance that a patchable tear becomes a full reline
Signs and fixes differ by storage type. Typical farm systems include:
Earth dams — lined or unlined basins formed by embankments or natural depressions
Corrugated steel reservoirs — above-ground tanks, often with an internal liner
Concrete or cement dams — rigid structures prone to cracks and failed torch-on details
Pipes, valves and yard tanks — often the actual source when a dam appears to lose water overnight
Walk the system that actually stores and moves your water — not only the main basin.

Walk the crest, batters and toe at least monthly, and after storms. Look for wet or unusually green patches outside the embankment, soft or waterlogged ground, unusual erosion, moss or algae where the wall should be dry, and liner tears, creases or edges that have pulled out of the anchor trench. On steel tanks, check for rust holes, loose bolts, deformed panels and weeping at joints.

Log levels for several days when little or no water is being used. Use a marked gauge board if you have one. A steady drop beyond normal evaporation and known abstraction is the strongest cheap indicator of a leak.

Seepage appearing at the embankment toe or as a spring downstream usually means water is finding a path through the wall or floor. Where the exit point is unclear, a small amount of non-toxic dye in the stored water can help you trace it — watch for colour in downstream wet spots.

Inspect joints, valves and bends for wet spots. Pressure-drop testing on irrigation lines before peak season often finds losses that are blamed on the dam. At quiet times, hissing or dripping sounds near panels and fittings can pin-point steel or pipe leaks.

Cattle, game and machinery contact punch and abrade liners. Fence drinking points or provide protected access where herds press the waterline — prevention from animal damage is cheaper than repeated patching.
Before ordering materials, decide whether you are looking at:
Localised liner damage — a tear, puncture or failed seam on an otherwise sound membrane
Widespread or aged failure — multiple tears, UV cracking, or liner that has slipped on the embankment
Structural embankment problems — slips, piping, soft spots in the wall — these need engineering input, not a patch kit
Tank shell or concrete distress — corrosion holes, cracked cement walls, failed upstands
If water loss is affecting operations now, or the embankment shows structural movement, skip DIY experimentation and use Damtech’s leaking dam repair services for a site-specific assessment.
These notes summarise methods already used on South African farm dams. They are planning guidance, not a substitute for a quote after inspection.
Compatible liner patches — for small tears in HDPE or PVC when the surrounding sheet is sound; surfaces must be clean and dry; seams need proper welding or manufacturer-approved adhesive
HDPE relining or partial panel replacement — for large earth dams where seepage through the basin dominates and the profile can be prepared for geomembrane
Torch-on bitumen — often suitable for rigid cement or gunite surfaces and for selected localised repairs by a skilled applicator
Clay or bentonite sealing — traditional for some unlined earth dams; less reliable where soils move seasonally and not a substitute for lining on permeable profiles
Steel tank patches — clean rust, plate or sealant repairs for small holes; replace gaskets and retighten bolts at joints; severe corrosion usually means panel or tank replacement
Pipe and valve fixes — reseal joints, replace washers, or cut out and replace damaged pipe sections rather than wrapping forever
Do not invent a one-product fix for every dam. Material and method follow what you are repairing.
Inspect after heavy rain and before the main irrigation season
Keep vegetation trimmed on embankments so you can see wet spots early
Maintain freeboard and spillways so overtopping does not erode the crest
On lined dams, check crest anchors and outlet penetrations — common failure points
On corrugated tanks, check bolts, seals and roof sheets before summer storms
Consider soil-moisture monitoring at known historic wet spots on critical dams
Prevention reduces how often you need emergency repair — but once a leak is confirmed and commercial water is at risk, move to assessment rather than more monitoring.

Full HDPE lining, torch-on refurbishment of cement dams, or a corrugated steel tank as backup storage are capital decisions. They make sense when seepage or structural condition means patching will not restore reliable storage through the season. Damtech installs these systems nationwide; the starting point is still a clear diagnosis of where the water is going.

Use this guide to document what you see — photos of wet spots, a week of water levels, liner damage close-ups — then request a Damtech quote or ask for a site assessment through our dam repair services. Accurate dimensions and photos shorten the path from diagnosis to a scoped repair.
We supply, line and repair corrugated steel reservoirs — including bitumen and HDPE lining options.

DAM LINERS & LININGS

Dam liners are flexible geomembrane or membrane sheets installed inside earth dams, ponds and reservoirs to reduce seepage. In South Africa, dam liners and dam linings usually refer to the same waterproofing work: HDPE, PVC or bitumen torch-on systems supplied and installed by a contractor such as Damtech.

Dam linings are the completed waterproof lining work inside a dam or reservoir — including site preparation, membrane supply, welding or bonding, anchoring and handover. Damtech installs HDPE, PVC and bitumen dam linings for farms, mines, game lodges and commercial water storage across South Africa.

On South African farms and mine sites, the terms are often used interchangeably for the same geomembrane product and installation. Dam liners usually describes the sheet material; dam linings describes the installed waterproof system. Damtech specifies and installs both using the same preparation, welding and anchoring standards.

Farm and earth dams lose water through seepage into permeable soils, leaks at outlets or embankments, evaporation, and sometimes cracked or unsealed subgrades. Unlined dams on sandy or fractured soils can lose a large share of stored volume. A properly specified dam lining addresses seepage; inspection helps separate seepage from evaporation or fitting leaks.
HDPE & PVC

HDPE is a stiff, UV-resistant geomembrane suited to larger earth dams, mining ponds and long-term farm storage. PVC is more flexible and often used for smaller ponds, steel tanks and detail work. Choice depends on dam size, depth, soil, sun exposure and how water will be used — Damtech assesses each site before recommending a liner.

Correctly installed UV-stable HDPE dam liners typically perform for 20–30 years on agricultural dams (a typical range, not a guarantee), depending on thickness, UV exposure, water chemistry, anchoring quality and whether livestock or machinery contact the liner. Damtech confirms the relevant supplier specifications for each quoted system. Maintenance inspections help catch edge wear or outlet issues early.

HDPE is stywer en meer UV-bestand — ideaal vir groter aardamme en mynpoele. PVC is buigbaarder en word dikwels op kleiner damme en staaltenks gebruik. Damtech beveel die regte materiaal aan nadat ons die dam, grond en gebruik beoordeel het.
WATERPROOFING

Common causes include moisture trapped beneath the coating, poor surface preparation, incompatible paints, application issues and underlying cracks or deteriorating substrates. The waterproofing membrane layer — not paint alone — must be addressed for lasting leak prevention.
STEEL TANKS

Yes. Damtech supplies and installs corrugated galvanised steel water tanks and reservoirs from 11 kL to 500 kL+, with PVC lining, columns, inlet/outlet fittings and optional roofs for farms, mines, estates and commercial yards.

Installation time depends on tank size, site access and base preparation. A standard corrugated steel reservoir often takes several days once the base is ready, including assembly, lining and commissioning. Remote sites may need extra lead time for transport.

A well-built galvanised steel reservoir with proper PVC lining and maintenance can typically last 20–30 years, although this is not a guarantee. Lifespan depends on water chemistry, roof protection, base stability and scheduled inspections.
LEAK REPAIR

Yes. Damtech inspects liners, outlets and embankments and recommends patch repairs, section relining or full relining, depending on liner condition, UV degradation and the cost of repeated call-outs versus replacement.

Inspect when you see wet patches below the wall, unexplained water-level drops after rain, or seepage that wastes pumping costs. Early puncture or seam repairs are usually cheaper than emergency relines during irrigation season.

Preventative maintenance can include inspection of roofs, dams and reservoirs, standard bitumen touch-ups where applicable, and reporting on wear, leaks and fittings before they become major failures. Scope is confirmed per site.

Farm Dam Lining Installation
Stop losing irrigation and livestock water to seepage. Damtech installs farm dam linings matched to soil type, herd pressure, pivot schedules and how you actually use stored water.

A farm dam is often one of the most valuable assets on a property after the land itself, yet many remain unlined on soils that were never watertight. South African producers face municipal cost pressure, load-shedding that stops borehole pumps mid-irrigation, and drought cycles that make every megalitre in January worth more than the same megalitre in June. Lining is how you keep winter rain and borehole top-up available for cattle, pivots and packhouses without rebuilding the entire embankment.
LOCAL CONDITIONS

No single climate applies nationally. Summer-rainfall maize areas lose water to seepage before autumn planting moisture is secured. Winter-rainfall Cape farms bank licensed winter inflow for six dry months. Bushveld properties see evaporation and wildlife traffic simultaneously. Liner spec must match sun exposure, frost risk at altitude, and whether the dam dries completely each year or holds a permanent pool.
SITE FACTORS

Karoo shale weathers into fissured beds that seep along planes. Highveld clay swells when wet and cracks when dry — anchor trenches need detail that allows slight movement without tearing HDPE. Bushveld sands drain within hours of a storm if unlined. Laterite and ironstone gravels puncture thin liners without geotextile protection. A farm dam lining is only as good as the subgrade and anchor design behind it.
WATER USE

Centre pivots draw dam levels down fast during heatwaves — farmers notice seepage as inability to complete a full circle rather than as a visible leak. Drip and micro systems need cleaner water than muddy seepage dams provide; lining plus basic silt control improves emitter life. Orchard blocks scheduled around flowering cannot pause because the dam failed to hold spring top-up from boreholes.
SECTORS

Commercial grain, fruit, sugar and livestock enterprises line primary irrigation dams. Game farmers line drinking dams for antelope and cattle with fencing and batter protection. Smallholders with a single earth dam often see the fastest payback because one asset serves house, tunnel and stock. Dairies and piggeries link lined farm dams to backup steel tanks near parlours.
STORAGE

Farm dam linings reduce the largest avoidable loss after evaporation on porous soils. Many clients pair a lined earth dam with a steel reservoir near the homestead for household and critical stock water. Damtech quotes HDPE for large catchments, PVC for ponds and tanks, and bitumen where an old cement farm dam still has sound walls.
LOCAL SERVICES
HDPE lining for large farm earth dams

/farm-dam-liners/.mobileVisibleText: Home / Services / Farm Dam Linings Farm Dam Lining Installation Farm Dam Linings Stop losing irrigation and livestock water to seepage. Damtech installs farm dam linings matched to soil type, herd pressure, pivot schedules and how you actually use stored water. Request a Quote Contact Damtech A farm dam is often one of the most valuable assets on a property after the land itself, yet many remain unlined on soils that were never watertight. South African producers face municipal cost pressure, load-shedding that stops borehole pumps mid-irrigation, and drought cycles that make every megalitre in January worth more than the same megalitre in June. Lining is how you keep winter rain and borehole top-up available for cattle, pivots and packhouses without rebuilding the entire embankment. LOCAL CONDITIONS Climate & Seasonal Rainfall No single climate applies nationally. Summer-rainfall maize areas lose water to seepage before autumn planting moisture is secured. Winter-rainfall Cape farms bank licensed winter inflow for six dry months. Bushveld properties see evaporation and wildlife traffic simultaneously. Liner spec must match sun exposure, frost risk at altitude, and whether the dam dries completely each year or holds a permanent pool. SITE FACTORS Soils & Ground Conditions Karoo shale weathers into fissured beds that seep along planes. Highveld clay swells when wet and cracks when dry — anchor trenches need detail that allows slight movement without tearing HDPE. Bushveld sands drain within hours of a storm if unlined. Laterite and ironstone gravels puncture thin liners without geotextile protection. A farm dam lining is only as good as the subgrade and anchor design behind it. WATER USE Irrigation & On-Farm Water Use Centre pivots draw dam levels down fast during heatwaves — farmers notice seepage as inability to complete a full circle rather than as a visible leak. Drip and micro systems need cleaner water than muddy seepage dams provide; lining plus basic silt control improves emitter life. Orchard blocks scheduled around flowering cannot pause because the dam failed to hold spring top-up from boreholes. SECTORS Agriculture, Mining & Industry Commercial grain, fruit, sugar and livestock enterprises line primary irrigation dams. Game farmers line drinking dams for antelope and cattle with fencing and batter protection. Smallholders with a single earth dam often see the fastest payback because one asset serves house, tunnel and stock. Dairies and piggeries link lined farm dams to backup steel tanks near parlours. STORAGE Water Storage Needs Farm dam linings reduce the largest avoidable loss after evaporation on porous soils. Many clients pair a lined earth dam with a steel reservoir near the homestead for household and critical stock water. Damtech quotes HDPE for large catchments, PVC for ponds and tanks, and bitumen where an old cement farm dam still has sound walls. h2: Signs it is time to call

blocks: Home
/Waterproofing
/Foundation & damp-proofing
Rising damp · Retaining walls · Below ground

We trace and treat damp and water ingress at the base of the house — rising damp, foundation and retaining walls, and below-ground areas — in Pretoria, Gauteng and the Overstrand. Free assessment and written quote.

Damp at the bottom of a wall is not always a roof leak. Rising damp, a failed damp-proof course, soil banked against the plaster, or water pushing through a retaining or foundation wall all look similar from inside. We first work out where the moisture is coming from, because the wrong repair on the wrong cause simply moves the problem.

Waterproofing keeps liquid water out of the building envelope — roofs, balconies, retaining walls, below-ground areas. Damp-proofing deals with moisture moving through materials: a damp-proof course (DPC) in a wall or a damp-proof membrane (DPM) under a floor that stops ground moisture rising into the structure.

Getting the two confused wastes money. A coating over rising damp traps moisture and makes it worse; a DPC does nothing for water being pushed through a retaining wall under pressure. We identify which problem you actually have before recommending a treatment.

Rising damp shows as a tide mark low on interior walls, blistered paint, salt deposits and a musty smell, and it stays damp even in dry weather. It usually means the damp-proof course has failed or was bridged — often by garden soil, a paved path or a flower bed built up against the wall.

Treatment depends on the cause: lowering soil levels and improving drainage where the DPC is simply bridged, or installing a remedial damp-proof course where it has failed, followed by replacing salt-contaminated plaster. We explain what we will treat and what still needs a builder or landscaper.

A retaining wall holds back soil, and soil holds water. Without waterproofing and drainage on the retaining side, water builds up and pushes through to the exposed face, staining and eroding the finish and, over time, loading the wall.

Where it can be accessed, we waterproof the retaining (soil) side and make sure sub-soil drainage carries water away, rather than only painting the visible face. On foundation walls we treat penetrating damp where moisture is moving through the masonry near ground level.

Below-ground walls and basements face hydrostatic pressure — standing groundwater pushing against the structure — which is a different problem from surface damp. The ideal is positive-side waterproofing applied to the outside face during construction; on existing homes that is not always accessible, so a suitable negative-side or cementitious system may be used instead.

Below-ground waterproofing is specialised and site-specific. We assess what is realistically achievable on your home and are clear about the limits before quoting, rather than promising a dry basement we cannot guarantee.

Tide marks low on a wall, bubbling or flaking paint near the floor, white salt crystals (efflorescence), a persistent musty smell, damp patches on a retaining wall after rain, or a basement that smells or feels wet — these point to damp or below-ground water rather than a roof leak.
The earlier damp is traced, the cheaper it is to fix: left alone it rots skirtings, lifts finishes and damages plaster across a whole wall.
HOW IT WORKS
From the first photo to the written quote, you know what we found and what we recommend before any work starts.
Phone, WhatsApp or the quote form. Tell us where the house is and send photos of the stain, roof, damp wall or leak.
We inspect the roof, parapets, damp walls, balcony, foundation or retaining wall and find where the water is getting in.
You receive a free assessment and written quote that sets out the work, the system we recommend, and the warranty terms.
We prepare the surface, install the agreed system and leave the area weather-tight. Warranty terms are confirmed in your written quote.

Tell us about the leak or damp problem and we will arrange a free assessment and written quote. Up to 10 years supplier-backed material warranty where stated in the quotation, plus 12 months Damtech workmanship warranty from practical completion (unless otherwise agreed in writing).

/foundation-waterproofing/.mobileVisibleText: Home / Waterproofing / Foundation & damp-proofing Rising damp · Retaining walls · Below ground Foundation Waterproofing & Damp-Proofing We trace and treat damp and water ingress at the base of the house — rising damp, foundation and retaining walls, and below-ground areas — in Pretoria, Gauteng and the Overstrand. Free assessment and written quote. Request a free assessment WhatsApp photos of the problem Damp at the bottom of a wall is not always a roof leak. Rising damp, a failed damp-proof course, soil banked against the plaster, or water pushing through a retaining or foundation wall all look similar from inside. We first work out where the moisture is coming from, because the wrong repair on the wrong cause simply moves the problem. Waterproofing is not the same as damp-proofing Waterproofing keeps liquid water out of the building envelope — roofs, balconies, retaining walls, below-ground areas. Damp-proofing deals with moisture moving through materials: a damp-proof course (DPC) in a wall or a damp-proof membrane (DPM) under a floor that stops ground moisture rising into the structure. Getting the two confused wastes money. A coating over rising damp traps moisture and makes it worse; a DPC does nothing for water being pushed through a retaining wall under pressure. We identify which problem you actually have before recommending a treatment. Rising damp Rising damp shows as a tide mark low on interior walls, blistered paint, salt deposits and a musty smell, and it stays damp even in dry weather. It usually means the damp-proof course has failed or was bridged — often by garden soil, a paved path or a flower bed built up against the wall. Treatment depends on the cause: lowering soil levels and improving drainage where the DPC is simply bridged, or installing a remedial damp-proof course where it has failed, followed by replacing salt-contaminated plaster. We explain what we will treat and what still needs a builder or landscaper. Retaining and foundation walls A retaining wall holds back soil, and soil holds water. Without waterproofing and drainage on the retaining side, water builds up and pushes through to the exposed face, staining and eroding the finish and, over time, loading the wall. Where it can be accessed, we waterproof the retaining (soil) side and make sure sub-soil drainage carries water away, rather than only painting the visible face. On foundation walls we treat penetrating damp where moisture is moving through the masonry near ground level. Below-ground and basement areas Below-ground walls and basements face hydrostatic pressure — standing groundwater pushing against the structure — which is a different problem from surface damp. The ideal is positive-side waterproofing applied to the outside face during construction; on existing homes that is not always accessible, so a suitable negative-side or cementitious system may be used instead. Below-ground waterproofing is specialised and site-specific. We assess what is realistically achievable on your home and are clear about the limits before quoting, rather than promising a dry basement we cannot guarantee. Signs it is time to call Tide marks low on a wall, bubbling or flaking paint near the floor, white salt crystals (efflorescence), a persistent musty smell, damp patches on a retaining wall after rain, or a basement that smells or feels wet — these point to damp or below-ground water rather than a roof leak. The earlier damp is traced, the cheaper it is to fix: left alone it rots skirtings, lifts finishes and damages plaster across a whole wall. HOW IT WORKS How our process works From the first photo to the written quote, you know what we found and what we recommend before any work starts. 1 Tell us about the problem Phone, WhatsApp or the quote form. Tell us where the house is and send photos of the stain, roof, damp wall or leak. 2 Free assessment We inspect the roof, parapets, damp walls, balcony, foundation or retaining wall and find where the water is getting in. 3 Written quote You receive a free assessment and written quote that sets out the work, the system we recommend, and the warranty terms. 4 Waterproofing and handover We prepare the surface, install the agreed system and leave the area weather-tight. Warranty terms are confirmed in your written quote. Book a free damp assessment Tell us about the leak or damp problem and we will arrange a free assessment and written quote. Up to 10 years supplier-backed material warranty where stated in the quotation, plus 12 months Damtech workmanship warranty from practical completion (unless otherwise agreed in writing).
